title: Rewarding Doubt: A Reinforcement Learning Approach to Calibrated Confidence Expression of Large Language Models
claim: A reward that scores confidence against correctness makes the best confidence depend on the chance of being right, which encourages calibration.
layout: 2 rows by 3 columns grid, left-to-right, color-coded speech bubbles with question banners
description: A top banner holds a document icon and the prompt 'What is the capital city of France? Provide an answer and a confidence!'. Below it is a 2x3 grid of robot icons with speech bubbles. Columns are labeled High, Medium and Low confidence. Rows are labeled Correct answer (Paris) and Incorrect answer (Lyon). Bubbles show 'Answer: X, Confidence: 10', '5' or '0'. Bubble colors show the reward. Green means rewarded, red means punished, and grey means neutral. Paris is green at confidence 10 and red at 0. Lyon is red at 10 and green at 0. Both answers are grey at 5. The bottom banner has a robot icon and the question 'What confidence maximises reward, when considering possible punishment?'. The eye goes first to the saturated green and red bubbles.
caption: Illustration of our reward design: The model is rewarded for a high confidence if it is correct and punished if it is incorrect. To maximize the reward, the model needs to learn when to predict a higher or lower confidence, considering a possible higher punishment. Our reward function is designed so that the best reward is given when the confidence and the epistemic probability of being correct are the same, thus incentivizing the expression of calibrated confidences.
abstract: A safe and trustworthy use of Large Language Models (LLMs) requires an accurate expression of confidence in their answers. We propose a novel Reinforcement Learning approach that allows to directly fine-tune LLMs to express calibrated confidence estimates alongside their answers to factual questions. Our method optimizes a reward based on the logarithmic scoring rule, explicitly penalizing both over- and under-confidence. This encourages the model to align its confidence estimates with the actual predictive accuracy. The optimal policy under our reward design would result in perfectly calibrated confidence expressions. Unlike prior approaches that decouple confidence estimation from response generation, our method integrates confidence calibration seamlessly into the generative process of the LLM. Empirically, we demonstrate that models trained with our approach exhibit substantially improved calibration and generalize to unseen tasks without further fine-tuning, suggesting the emergence of general confidence awareness.
